lesson.title: Loading the Truck: What Transmission Delay Really Measures
lesson.summary: Transmission delay is the time a sender needs to push every bit of a packet onto the link, set entirely by packet size and bandwidth.
lesson.body:
Transmission delay is the time it takes for a sending device to push every bit of a packet onto the outgoing link. It is not about how far the data has to travel. It is about how fast the sender can physically place the bits on the wire, fiber, or radio channel. The formula is simple: transmission delay equals packet size in bits divided by the link's bandwidth in bits per second. A bigger packet takes longer to push out. A faster link pushes the same packet out sooner.

This is where transmission delay connects directly to bandwidth. Bandwidth describes the maximum rate at which bits can be placed onto a link, and transmission delay is simply the consequence of that rate applied to a specific packet size. Transmission delay is also only one piece of latency, the total time a packet takes to get from source to destination. Latency also includes propagation delay, the time for a signal to travel the physical distance of the link at close to the speed of light, along with queuing and processing delays covered in the next two chapters. Transmission delay and propagation delay are easy to confuse because both happen on every link, but they measure different things: one is about packet size and link speed, the other is about distance and the medium's signal speed.

Consider a typical 1500 byte packet, the common maximum size on Ethernet networks, sent over a 100 Mbps link. First convert bytes to bits: 1500 bytes times 8 equals 12,000 bits. Divide by the bandwidth: 12,000 bits divided by 100,000,000 bits per second equals 0.00012 seconds, or 120 microseconds. That is how long the sender's network interface spends physically transmitting that one packet before it can start the next one.

Now shrink the link speed. Send the same 12,000 bit packet over an old 1 Mbps connection instead. The transmission delay becomes 12,000 divided by 1,000,000, which is 0.012 seconds, or 12 milliseconds. That is one hundred times longer than on the 100 Mbps link, even though the packet did not change size at all and the distance to the destination did not change either. This is why upgrading bandwidth reduces transmission delay directly, while it does nothing to reduce propagation delay, which depends on distance instead.

Transmission delay happens again at every hop along a path, not just at the source. Routers typically use store and forward switching: a router must receive an entire packet, check it, and then transmit that same packet in full onto the next link before moving on. That means the 120 microsecond transmission delay from the earlier example gets paid again, using the outgoing link's own bandwidth, at every router between source and destination. On a path through five routers, five separate transmission delays are incurred, one for each link, and they can differ if the links have different bandwidths.

Understanding transmission delay matters because it is the delay component an engineer can most directly control by upgrading equipment. You cannot shorten the distance to a server across the ocean, but you can install a faster link and shrink transmission delay immediately. Keep this distinction in mind as we look at queuing delay and processing delay next: together with transmission delay and propagation delay, they add up to the total delay a packet experiences at each hop, and summing those hop by hop delays across a path is exactly what produces the end to end latency you measure in practice.
